findings.body:
**Issue:** `log.debug` includes `process.env.PROCESSOR_KEY` in the structured payload on every charge. That credential will land in log sinks (stdout, agents, support tooling) whenever debug logging is enabled — including staging and incident debugging — and anyone with log access can reuse it against the payment processor.

**Failure mode:** A single charge in an environment with debug logs on exfiltrates the live processor key via normal log shipping; no exploit of the app itself is required.

**Fix:** Keep logging only non-sensitive charge context (`orderId`, `ref`). If support needs replay, use the `ref` with a secured internal path that reads the key from the secret store at call time. Never put credentials in log fields.

```suggestion
  log.info("charge created", { orderId: order.id, ref });
```

summary:
## Verdict

**Do not merge** — this change logs the payment processor credential (`PROCESSOR_KEY`) into application debug payloads on every successful charge.

## Narrative

`charge()` previously emitted a non-sensitive info log (`orderId`, `ref`). The new debug line intentionally attaches `process.env.PROCESSOR_KEY` so support can "replay failures." That puts a live processor secret into whatever sink backs `log.debug` (stdout, aggregated logs, log vendors, support tooling). Anyone with log read access can exfiltrate the key and create charges outside this service.

Debug level does not make this safe: many environments enable debug in staging or during incident response, and log pipelines often retain debug events. Support replay should use an existing charge `ref` / order id plus a secured internal tool that holds credentials server-side — never by copying the key into log lines.

No redaction layer is present in this tree around `log`, so the value would be written as-is.

## Release decision

**Recommendation:** request-changes
